metadata.title: Imageomics Guide
metadata.description:
Imageomics-focused guide to collaborative work, including GitHub and Hugging Face workflows. 

The website hosts Imageomics-focused guides to FAIR (findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable) and reproducible workflows, documentation, and general best-practices for collaborative science. We aim to provide a helpful resource for scientists working in imageomics and related interdisciplinary fields.

Website: imageomics.github.io/Imageomics-guide/

This guide houses the information needed to get started with and use Imageomics Institute resources readily available to all members. However, most of this guide is applicable to anyone working more broadly in the field of imageomics or adjacent fields of computer and data science, and it is tailored to help domain scientists bridging that gap.
references: Campolongo, E. G., Thompson, M. J., Zhang, N., Duan, Y., Bradley, J., Zarubiieva, I., Taylor, G., & Lapp, H. (2026). Collaborative Distributed Science Guide (Version 2.0.0) [Computer software]. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17210328

metadata.title: biocorecrg/scnanoseq: v1.0.0
metadata.description:
🎉 Initial Release: v1.0.0

First public release of scnanoseq — A comprehensive Nextflow pipeline for Oxford Nanopore single-cell RNA-sequencing with support for multiple sequencing platforms.

Features

  • Multi-platform support: Process data from 10X Genomics (3' and 5' protocols), Argentag, and Parse single-cell sequencing platforms
  • Platform-specific demultiplexing: Dedicated workflows for each platform including barcode detection, extraction, and correction
  • Comprehensive quality control: Multi-stage QC with FastQC, NanoPlot, NanoComp, ToulligQC, and RSeQC
  • Flexible quantification: Support for both IsoQuant (gene + transcript level) and oarfish (transcript level) for feature-barcode matrix generation
  • Reproducible analysis: Container-based workflow with Docker/Singularity support and comprehensive parameter documentation
  • Test datasets: Pre-configured test datasets with example samplesheets and parameter files for all platforms
  • Detailed documentation: Complete README with platform-specific usage examples, output descriptions, and troubleshooting guides

Installation

Requirements:

  • Nextflow (requires Java 11+)
  • Docker or Singularity for container support

Quick Start:

# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/biocorecrg/scnanoseq.git
cd scnanoseq

# Run the pipeline
nextflow run main.nf \
   -profile docker \
   -params-file params.yaml

See the README for detailed installation and usage instructions for each platform.

Requirements

  • Nextflow: ≥24.04.2
  • Container engine: Docker or Singularity
  • Java: 11 or later
  • Storage: Minimum 200GB for full analysis runs
  • Compute: 36-72 hours runtime per platform analysis on typical HPC clusters

Known Issues

  • Parse platform test datasets: 1M read test datasets may not contain sufficient reads after preprocessing for split-pipe. Use ≥2M reads or full datasets for reliable Parse testing. See README for details.
  • None other reported yet — please report bugs and issues via GitHub Issues!

What's New

This is the first public release of the CRG fork extending the original nf-core/scnanoseq pipeline with:

  • Full support for Argentag single-cell sequencing platform with taggy_demux v1.1 demultiplexing
  • Full support for Parse single-cell sequencing platform with parse_pe_ont v4.0 and split-pipe v1.6.1
  • Comprehensive test datasets and parameter files for all three platforms
  • Enhanced documentation with platform-specific examples and considerations

Documentation

  • README — Complete usage guide with platform-specific instructions
  • Output Documentation — Detailed description of all output files and directories
  • CITATIONS.md — References for all tools and methods used

Benchmarking

Analysis of full datasets (3 replicates per platform) was performed using:

  • Reference genomes: Human (GRCh38), Mouse (GRCm39), Dog (ROS_Cfam_1.0) from Ensembl v111
  • Platform runtimes: 36-72 hours per platform on CRG HPC (variation based on resource availability)

See README for complete dataset specifications and analysis details.

Credits

  • Original pipeline: Austyn Trull and Dr. Lara Ianov
  • Argentag and Parse support: Anna Delgado — Bioinformatics Unit, Centre for Genomic Regulation (CRG)

Support

For issues, questions, or feature requests, please:

  • Open an issue on GitHub
  • Check the README troubleshooting section

Ready to get started? See the README for installation and usage instructions!

metadata.title: musicalgestures: A Python toolbox for visualising and analysing music-related video recordings
metadata.description: This is the Python version of the Musical Gestures Toolbox, containing a complete solution for loading different types of video recordings (including 360-degree videos). It was originally built to analyse music-related videos, but it works well for many other applications. It includes a large collection of tools for visualising human body motion, including average images, motion images, motion history images, motiongrams, and videograms. It also includes spatial–temporal tools for creating motion history videos. Finally, it wraps different state-of-the-art pose estimation methods (CV2 and MediaPipe) and derives various quantity-of-motion measures.

metadata.title: Replication package of 'Systematic Detection of Energy Regressions in Software Version Histories'
metadata.description:
This upload includes the energy measurements results collected using the EnergyTrackr pipeline, supporting the paper Systematic Detection of Energy Regressions in Software Version Histories, submitted to the Green Software Evolution special issue of the Information and Software Technology journal.

The dataset aims to facilitate reproducibility and future research on energy-aware software development and the identification of energy regressions. The analysis covers 5 projects: Classgraph, Fastexcel, Maker, Modelmapper and Simple-OpenAI. Each project directory contains the configuration files used for both algorithms, along with two subdirectories: dichotomous-data and naive-data. These subdirectories include all generated data obtained through the respective algorithms. Each subdirectory contains 4 files: a CSV file with raw data, a CSV file with sorted raw data, an HTML file generated by EnergyTrackr, and a log file containing all execution logs.

metadata.title: flask-todolist — a small application carrying a large, machine-checked governance apparatus
metadata.description:
A Flask to-do application used as the substrate for an experiment in machine-checked project governance.

Every rule the project declares is indexed in a registry (gates.yaml) verified in both directions; each rule must carry evidence that it once failed for a real defect (proved_by); the portable subset is generated into an agent skill and an overlay applicable to other projects; and the effect on generated code is measured against controlled arms. 27 recorded audit rounds, each asking a question the previous round could not, are part of the artefact.

Documentation and the decision records are licensed CC BY-SA 4.0; the software is AGPL-3.0-or-later.

metadata.title: CroCoDeEL: Cross-sample Contamination Detection and Estimation of its Level
metadata.description:
Performance

  • Contamination search is about 4.5 times faster: on a 237-sample dataset it now takes 12.5 seconds instead of 58 seconds using 8 CPUs, with identical results

Bug fixes

  • easy_wf again exposes only the three mandatory files (-s, -c, -r); use search_conta and plot_conta to change any other setting
  • Fixed scatterplots being wrong when a second abundance table is provided: species absent from one table were drawn at 100% abundance instead of being treated as absent
  • Made contamination event ordering deterministic, so identical inputs always produce identical output files
  • Contamination rates of zero are no longer reported or accepted
  • No PDF report is written when no contamination is found, instead of an unreadable empty file
  • --nproc now defaults to the CPUs actually available to the process, rather than every core on the machine, and an existing OMP_NUM_THREADS setting is preserved

Improved error handling

  • Malformed species abundance tables (empty or with an inconsistent number of columns) now report a clear message instead of a traceback
  • Malformed contamination event files are rejected with the offending line number, including rows with missing or extra fields
  • Contamination event files that name samples absent from the abundance table are rejected before the report is generated
  • Invalid Random Forest model files are rejected before the search starts
  • Species abundance tables containing missing values are rejected
  • Error messages listing many sample names are truncated instead of printing thousands of names on one line

Other

  • Replaced scikit-learn's RANSAC with a specialised implementation in a dedicated module, giving identical results
  • Added mypy and pylint to the continuous integration workflow
  • Added Python 3.13 to the test matrix and restricted supported versions to 3.12–3.13
  • Added unit tests, bringing coverage to 98%
  • Refactored the command-line interface, packaged-resource handling and execution description

metadata.title: Open Analysis and Reproducibility Materials for Component-Specific Changes in Football Execution Speed and Response Accuracy in Under-9 Players
metadata.description:
This record contains open analysis and reproducibility materials associated with a prospective, non-randomised comparative cohort study of two academy football training programmes in 25 male under-9 players. Thirteen players completed a structured tactical reflection/game-centred programme and 12 followed their academy’s usual repetition-oriented programme; one comparison-cohort participant did not complete post-testing.

Football-specific performance was assessed before and after 12 training sessions using the Stroop Task Football Test (STFT). The registered primary outcome was the Total Index (TI). Execution time (ET), type-of-action accuracy (TA), direction-of-movement accuracy (DM), and total correct responses were analysed as additional component outcomes.

The archive includes the data dictionary, complete analysis code, declared software dependencies, full statistical output, publication figures, an individual-trajectory supplementary figure, reproducibility notes, and file-integrity checks. Source ET values were recorded in minutes and converted to seconds for manuscript reporting; TI retains the original calculation of total correct responses divided by ET in minutes.

Participant-level data are intentionally excluded from this public archive because the participants are minors. De-identified data may be made available to qualified researchers following review of a methodologically sound proposal and completion of an appropriate data-use agreement, in accordance with the registered data-sharing conditions.

Because each programme was delivered in one academy cohort, programme and academy context are structurally confounded. The materials reproduce the reported cohort-associated changes and robustness analyses but do not establish an academy-independent causal programme effect.

ClinicalTrials.gov registration: NCT07479368.

metadata.title: Integrating systematic conservation planning within marine spatial planning to strengthen marine conservation
metadata.description:
This repository contains the R scripts used to develop Species Distribution Models (SDMs) and implement Systematic Conservation Planning (SCP) for marine biodiversity across three Mediterranean pilot areas: the Northern Tyrrhenian Sea (NTS), Northern Adriatic Sea (NAS), and Strait of Sicily (SoS).

The workflow is organized into two main components. First, SDMs are developed for 39 marine species using species occurrence records and environmental predictors. Occurrence data are spatially thinned, and environmental predictors are screened for multicollinearity before model calibration. Species distributions are modelled under present environmental conditions using Random Forest, MaxNet, and XGBoost, and ensemble predictions are generated based on model performance. Species distributions are also projected under the SSP5 future climate scenario. The resulting species distribution layers are used as biodiversity features in the subsequent conservation planning analyses

Second, the SDM-derived species distributions are combined with seabed habitats and Essential Fish Habitats to define the conservation features used in the SCP analyses. These are integrated with conservation targets, spatial connectivity, existing and scenario-specific protected areas, and socio-economic cost layers representing three future Maritime Spatial Planning scenarios. The prioritization analyses generate alternative spatial solutions using prioritizr, including solutions based on unitary conservation costs and solutions incorporating scenario-specific socio-economic costs. Solutions are evaluated in terms of the number of selected planning units, associated costs, spatial connectivity, and the number of conservation features meeting their representation targets. Analyses are conducted using both present species-distribution outputs and future species-distribution projections under SSP5.

metadata.title: VECTRI-ABM
metadata.description: An agent-based model of disease transmission coupled to the VECTRI vector-ecology model (Tompkins et al. 2013). The framework resolves individual human agents on a climate-driven grid, with age-structured diagnostics including per-timestep symptomatic and asymptomatic incidence & age-dependent acquisition and waning of immunity. Calibration tools - Sobol sensitivity analysis (SALiB), a genetic algorithm (Tompkins et al. 2018) and an integration to the Optuna calibration suite are included. Agent mobility is defined but not yet functional. The underlying agent-based framework is named MoBILE (Mobility-Based Integrated Landscape Epidemiology), which remains the repository name; VECTRI-ABM is the vector-borne disease model built on it.

metadata.title: bhima_processing: analysis code for GEB-PlantFATE v1.0 afforestation scenarios
metadata.description:
Analysis and figure code for a coupled GEB-PlantFATE study of afforestation in the Ghod subbasin, Maharashtra, India.

Stefaniak, E. Z., Joshi, J., Artuso, S., Maxwell, T. L., Smilovic, M., Hofhansl, F., and de Bruijn, J. A.: GEB-PlantFATE v1.0: Coupling of forest demographic and soil hydrological models for simulating the hydrological impacts of afforestation and biodiversity. [JOURNAL / STATUS — ADD DOI WHEN AVAILABLE]

Processes daily model output for twelve afforestation and biodiversity scenarios into catchment-scale aggregates, spatial diagnostics and publication figures. Model output is archived separately at doi:10.5281/zenodo.18457345.

What this is

This repository processes raw GEB-PlantFATE model output into the catchment-scale aggregates, spatial diagnostics and publication figures reported in the paper. It contains code and one small spatial file; the model output itself is archived separately at 10.5281/zenodo.18457345 and must be downloaded to run the pipeline.

The underlying study applies the coupled GEB-PlantFATE model to a 628 km² section of the Ghod subbasin in Maharashtra, western India, across twelve scenarios combining six afforestation levels with high-biodiversity (10 species), low-biodiversity (1 species) and no-PlantFATE model setups, forced with ISIMIP3b GFDL-ESM4 output under SSP3-7.0 over 2020–2049.

Contents

Both R and Python are used. R handles most time-series processing and plotting; Python handles Zarr access, spatial operations and map production. Two Google Earth Engine JavaScript files export biomass reference layers and are run in the GEE code editor rather than locally.

- code/ — preprocessing, aggregation and PlantFATE diagnostics
- code/figures_publication/ — one script per publication figure
- code/google_earth_engine/ — GEE export scripts
- code/util/ — cell-list generation and Zarr packing helpers
- data/maps/region.gpkg — study area boundary

The pipeline runs in four broad stages: configuration and spatial setup; aggregation of daily gridded output to basin-wide and yearly summaries; extraction of per-cell environmental forcing and single-cell PlantFATE re-runs; and figure production.

## Requirements

Python ≥ 3.13, managed with uv (uv sync); dependencies pinned in uv.lock. R packages are not pinned — see the README for the list. All scripts are run from the repository root. Full setup instructions, the data download and extraction steps, the figure-to-script mapping, and known issues are in README.md.

Data not redistributed

Figure A2 uses relative density and dominance tables from appendices 3 and 4 of Jezeera (2016), which remain the copyright of the author and are not included here. The README explains how to obtain them.

Related resources

- Model output: doi:10.5281/zenodo.18457345
- GEB: v0.4, doi:10.5281/zenodo.22094305 — https://github.com/GEB-model/GEB
- PlantFATE: [DOI PENDING] — https://github.com/jaideep777/Plant-FATE
- GEB documentation: https://docs.geb.sh/
- Regional context: Kanade et al. (2023), doi:10.5281/zenodo.8255959

Funding

International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis, Strategic Initiatives Program — projects RESIST and FairStream.

Licence

GNU General Public License v3.0.

metadata.title: verifiable-gates — a rule catalogue where every rule carries the incident that produced it
metadata.description:
A catalogue of production-discipline rules for software projects, extracted from a reference implementation where each one was learned from a real failure. Every rule records the incident behind it, so a reader can judge whether the conditions that produced it still hold; a rule with no incident is a preference, and preferences do not earn a gate.

A rule and its enforcement are kept in separate files because they have separate lifetimes. The bundle ships nine standalone checkers that decide part of the catalogue mechanically in a project that has installed nothing, an installer and a doctor that run them, and a renderer that turns the catalogue into rule sheets an AI coding agent can be handed. The reference implementation is held to every rule published here, and a test in that project checks both directions.

metadata.title: QCima Studio
metadata.description:
QCima Studio is a standalone software application for quality control of MACSima spatial proteomics datasets. It provides convenient access to review individual antibody signals alongside their corresponding background and autofluorescence reference images.

Users can adjust visualization settings, classify signals as accepted or discarded, and automatically organize imaging data by scene (Rack–Well–ROI), antibody, and autofluorescence reference.

The software is designed for fast, script-free QC workflows and supports session saving, analysis resumption, structured metadata review, and seamless transfer of QC decisions back to MACS iQ View.
